title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18‑20 year‑olds will not get bigger increase
tldr: The UK Budget will raise the national minimum wage, but the increase for 18‑20 year‑olds will be modest (≈3.9 %) compared with the 26 % boost seen since 2024, while older workers receive a larger rise to £13.20. The government also announced a suite of cost‑of‑living measures, including tariff cuts on 100 food items and reforms to carer allowances, aiming to provide households with “breathing space” amid ongoing inflation pressures.
background: Chancellor John Healey’s first full Budget follows a period of heightened living‑cost pressures. Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledged to eliminate “discriminatory age bands” in the minimum wage, a promise that has been rolled out gradually. The latest figures from The Times suggest the government is now balancing that pledge against fiscal constraints, delivering a smaller increase for younger workers while still boosting the National Living Wage for those aged 21 and over. Simultaneously, Healey’s team is rolling out targeted relief—removing import duties on staple foods, extending the 5p fuel‑duty discount, and reforming carer‑allowance taper rules—to cushion households from inflation and supply‑chain shocks.

analysis.heading: Policy Design and Equity Considerations
analysis.content: The differential increase for 18‑20 year‑old workers reflects a pragmatic compromise between the Labour government’s egalitarian manifesto commitment and the fiscal reality of a tight budget. By aligning the younger cohort’s rise with the overall minimum‑wage growth (3.9 %), the Treasury avoids a sudden, large fiscal outlay that could destabilise public finances. However, this approach reignites the long‑standing debate over age‑based wage discrimination. Unions such as Unison argue that the same job should command the same pay, regardless of age, and point to the broader economic context where inflation erodes real wages across the board. The government’s justification—that the equalisation can be achieved “over time”—suggests a phased implementation strategy, which may be politically palatable but risks prolonging perceived inequity.

analysis.heading: Socio‑Economic Impact on Young Workers and Households
analysis.content: For 18‑20 year‑old employees in sectors like care, education support, and security, the projected rise from £10.85 to £11.27 per hour will still be below the National Living Wage of £13.20. While the absolute increase is modest, the broader cost‑of‑living package—including tariff removals on items such as baked beans, garlic, and plant‑based drinks—could offset the gap. The government estimates savings of up to £21 per year per household from these import duty cuts, complemented by the permanent 55p‑per‑mile tax‑free mileage rate and expanded paternity pay for the self‑employed. These measures collectively aim to improve disposable income for younger, often lower‑earning households, potentially mitigating the impact of stagnant wage growth in a high‑inflation environment.

analysis.heading: International Comparative Perspective and Fiscal Sustainability
analysis.content: The UK’s approach contrasts with several European neighbours that have adopted more aggressive minimum‑wage adjustments to counter inflation. Countries such as Germany and France have implemented sector‑wide wage floors that rise in line with productivity and inflation indices, often exceeding 5 % annually. The UK’s 3.9 % increase for older workers aligns more closely with these benchmarks, while the lower uplift for younger workers may be viewed as a compromise to maintain competitiveness in labour‑intensive service industries. From a fiscal sustainability standpoint, the government’s mixed strategy—targeted tariff reductions and selective wage hikes—seeks to balance short‑term relief with long‑term budgetary discipline, especially as borrowing costs remain elevated. However, critics argue that the piecemeal nature of the relief measures may be insufficient to address structural cost pressures, particularly for vulnerable groups such as carers and low‑income families.

key_facts: The National Minimum Wage for 18‑20 year‑olds is set to rise by 3.9 % from £10.85 to about £11.27 per hour.
The National Living Wage for workers aged 21+ will increase by 3.9 % to £13.20 per hour.
Since Labour returned to power in 2024, younger workers have seen a cumulative 26 % increase in their minimum wage.
The government will remove import tariffs on 100 food items, potentially saving households up to £21 per year.
Fuel duty will be frozen again, with the existing 5p per litre discount extended.
A permanent 55p‑per‑mile tax‑free mileage rate will apply up to 10,000 miles, with a higher rate beyond that.
Carer allowance taper reforms are slated for 2030, allowing carers to earn more without losing the full benefit.
Self‑employed fathers will receive two weeks of paternity pay, up to £194 per week.
implications: Younger workers may continue to face a wage gap relative to older colleagues, potentially affecting recruitment in care and support sectors.
Household savings from tariff cuts and fuel‑duty freezes could provide modest relief but may be offset by ongoing inflation in other goods.
The delayed carer‑allowance taper until 2030 suggests a cautious fiscal approach, but could postpone much‑needed support for informal carers.
The expansion of paternity pay for the self‑employed signals a broadening of social‑security coverage, aligning with broader labour‑market modernisation goals.
outlook: The Budget’s blend of modest wage adjustments and targeted cost‑of‑living relief reflects a cautious balancing act. While the measures may ease immediate financial pressures, the persistent differential in minimum‑wage growth could sustain industrial discontent and calls for legislative reform. Monitoring will be required to assess whether the tariff removals and fuel‑duty extensions sufficiently cushion households against inflation, and how the phased carer‑allowance changes impact the supply of unpaid care in an ageing society.
